# Data

Every chart reads its data from the `data` prop on `Chart`. Marks, axes, and legends inside it name the fields they use.

## Shape

`data` is a flat array of objects, one per data point. Each object has the same fields, and each value is a string, number, boolean, or `null`:

```ts
const data = [
  { date: '2026-03-02T00:00:00', device: 'Desktop', visits: 3120 },
  { date: '2026-03-02T00:00:00', device: 'Mobile', visits: 2280 },
  { date: '2026-03-03T00:00:00', device: 'Desktop', visits: 3480 },
  { date: '2026-03-03T00:00:00', device: 'Mobile', visits: 2410 },
];
```

Use one row per point, not one row per date with a column per series. A line chart with two series has a row for each series at each date, as above.

## Field names

Marks take the names of the fields to draw:

-   `dimension`: the field for the x-axis, or the categories.
-   `metric`: the numeric field that sets each point's value.
-   `color`: the field that splits rows into series. Each distinct value gets its own color and legend entry.

```tsx
<Chart data={data}>
  <Line dimension="date" metric="visits" color="device" />
</Chart>
```

If your data already uses the default names, you can leave the props off. `Line` reads `datetime` and `value`, `Bar` reads `category` and `value`, and `Donut` reads `value` and colors by `series`. Without `color`, `Line` and `Bar` draw every row as one series. Each chart's page lists its fields and defaults: [Line](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/line#data), [Bar](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/bar#data), [Donut](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/donut#data).

## Dates

Pass dates as milliseconds since the epoch, like `Date.now()` returns. ISO strings, like `'2026-03-02T09:00:00'`, also work on time scales; they're parsed with the browser's `Date`.

`Chart` copies `data` with `JSON.stringify`, so `Date` objects become ISO strings. Convert dates to timestamps before you pass them in.

Dates display in the user's local time zone. A timestamp at UTC midnight, or a date-only string like `'2026-03-02'` (which parses as UTC), shows as the previous day in time zones west of UTC. For daily data, use timestamps for local midnight or include a time in the string, like the examples on this page.

## Missing values

To leave a value out of an `Area`, set it to `null`. A stacked `Area` treats it as 0, and a floating `Area` leaves a gap ([Area](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/area#missing-values)). `undefined` and `NaN` are treated the same as `null`. A `Line` doesn't support gaps yet; leave the row out and the line connects the points on either side.

## Reserved fields

The chart adds fields to each row as it draws. Don't use these names in your data:

-   Any field that starts with `rsc`, like `rscMarkId` and `rscSeriesId`.
-   `datetime0` and `datetime1`, on charts with a time scale.
-   The metric name followed by `0` or `1`, like `value0` and `value1`, on stacked bars and areas.

## Row IDs

The chart gives each row its own ID. To refer to rows from outside the chart, for example with `highlightedItem`, give each row a unique ID field and name it with `idKey` on `Chart`. See [idKey](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#idkey).

## Empty data and loading

An empty `data` array shows an empty state with `emptyStateText` instead of the chart. Set `loading` while you fetch data to show a progress circle. See [Empty and loading](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#empty-and-loading).

## Updating data

To update the chart, pass a new array. The chart compares the new rows with the ones it's showing: equal rows do nothing, and changed rows update the current view in place. It doesn't notice changes made to the same array in place.

Comparing large datasets on every render has a cost, so keep `data` stable across renders. Build it outside the component, or memoize it:

```tsx
const data = useMemo(() => rows.map((row) => ({ ...row, date: Date.parse(row.date) })), [rows]);
```

Updating data in place doesn't replay the draw-in animation; see [Animation](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/guides/animation). Changes that need a new view, such as different children, call `onVegaViewReady` with the new view.

---

# Sizing

A chart fills the width of its container and is 300px tall unless you set `width` and `height` on `Chart`. This page covers how those props work together. See [Size](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#size) for a live example and the [Chart API](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#api) for each prop.

## Width

`width` takes one of:

-   `'auto'` (default): the container's width.
-   A number of pixels, like `600`.
-   A whole-number percentage of the container's width, like `'75%'`.

`Chart` watches its container with a `ResizeObserver`, so `auto` and percentage widths follow the container as it resizes. Resizing updates the chart in place; it doesn't redraw it or replay the draw-in animation.

`minWidth` (default `100`) and `maxWidth` (default none) clamp `auto` and percentage widths. They don't change a pixel `width`.

```tsx
<Chart data={data} maxWidth={960}>
  {/* ... */}
</Chart>
```

> **Note:**
> 
> A chart in a container with no width, like one inside an element with `display: none`, isn't drawn. It draws when the container gets a width.

## Height

`height` takes a number of pixels (default `300`) or a whole-number percentage of the container's height, like `'100%'`. There's no `auto` height.

A percentage height needs a container with an explicit height. The chart can't measure a container that's sized by its content, and isn't drawn.

```tsx
<div style={{ height: 400 }}>
  <Chart data={data} height="100%">
    {/* ... */}
  </Chart>
</div>
```

`minHeight` (default `100`) and `maxHeight` (default none) clamp a percentage height. They don't change a pixel `height`.

## What the size includes

`width` and `height` are the size of the whole chart: axes, legend, title, and `padding`. The plot area gets the space that's left, so adding a legend or a title makes the plot smaller.

`padding` adds space between the chart's edge and its contents, as one number or per side, like `{ top: 8, left: 16 }`. See [Padding](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#padding).

## Size tiers

Some styles scale with the chart's width, in three tiers:

| Tier | Chart width | Line stroke | Line points | Direct label text |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S | Under 400px | 1.5px | 6px | 14px |
| M | 400px to 799px | 2px | 8px | 16px |
| L | 800px and over | 2.5px | 10px | 18px |

The tier applies to line strokes and their hover and highlight states, line points, and the text of `LineDirectLabel`, `BarDirectLabel`, and `ReferenceLine` labels. It updates as the chart resizes. To fix a size instead, set `pointSize` on `Line` or `fontSize` on `LineDirectLabel`. See [Line size](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/line#size).

`Donut` sizes itself differently: its ring, labels, and `DonutSummary` scale with the smaller of the chart's width and height (twice the height for a semicircle). See [Donut size](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/donut#size).

---

# Colors and theming

A chart's colors come from three places: the color scheme (`light` or `dark`), the chart's palettes and style scales, and the encodings on each mark. This guide covers how they fit together. For the full prop reference, see [Chart](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#color-and-theme).

```jsx
import {
  Axis,
  Bar,
  Chart,
  Legend,
} from '@spectrum-charts/react-spectrum-charts-s2';

<Chart data={guideSourceSessionsData}>
  <Axis position="left" grid />
  <Axis position="bottom" baseline />
  <Bar dimension="quarter" metric="sessions" color="source" />
  <Legend />
</Chart>
```

The interactive example has these controls. The code above uses the shown values.

-   `colors` on `Chart`: `s2Categorical6`, `s2Categorical12`, `s2Categorical16`, `s2Categorical20`, `divergentOrangeYellowSeafoam5`, `divergentOrangeYellowSeafoam9`, `divergentOrangeYellowSeafoam15`, `divergentRedBlue5`, `divergentRedBlue9`, `divergentRedBlue15`, `divergentRedYellowBlue5`, `divergentRedYellowBlue9`, `divergentRedYellowBlue15`, `sequentialViridis5`, `sequentialViridis9`, `sequentialViridis16`, `sequentialMagma5`, `sequentialMagma9`, `sequentialMagma16`, `sequentialRose5`, `sequentialRose9`, `sequentialRose16`, `sequentialCerulean5`, `sequentialCerulean9`, `sequentialCerulean16`, `sequentialForest5`, `sequentialForest9` or `sequentialForest16`. Shown: `s2Categorical20`.
-   `backgroundColor` on `Chart`: `transparent`, `gray-25`, `gray-100` or `blue-100`. Shown: `transparent`.

The example uses `guideSourceSessionsData`:

```ts
const guideSourceSessionsData = [
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Search', sessions: 4200 },
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Direct', sessions: 3100 },
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Social', sessions: 2400 },
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Email', sessions: 1500 },
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Referral', sessions: 1100 },
  { quarter: 'Q1', source: 'Paid', sessions: 800 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Search', sessions: 4600 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Direct', sessions: 3300 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Social', sessions: 2900 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Email', sessions: 1400 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Referral', sessions: 1200 },
  { quarter: 'Q2', source: 'Paid', sessions: 1000 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Search', sessions: 4900 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Direct', sessions: 3200 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Social', sessions: 3400 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Email', sessions: 1600 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Referral', sessions: 1300 },
  { quarter: 'Q3', source: 'Paid', sessions: 1200 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Search', sessions: 5300 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Direct', sessions: 3600 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Social', sessions: 3800 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Email', sessions: 2100 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Referral', sessions: 1400 },
  { quarter: 'Q4', source: 'Paid', sessions: 1500 },
];
```

## Light and dark

`colorScheme` sets whether the chart uses the light or dark value of each Spectrum color token, for marks, axes, gridlines, and text. It defaults to `light`.

`Chart` renders its own React Spectrum `Provider` with this `colorScheme`, so it doesn't pick up the color scheme of a `Provider` higher in your app. Pass the same value to both, usually from your app's theme state:

```tsx
import { Provider } from '@react-spectrum/s2';
import { Axis, Chart, Line } from '@spectrum-charts/react-spectrum-charts-s2';

function Dashboard({ colorScheme }: { colorScheme: 'light' | 'dark' }) {
  return (
    <Provider colorScheme={colorScheme}>
      <Chart data={data} colorScheme={colorScheme}>
        <Axis position="left" grid />
        <Line dimension="month" metric="visits" color="device" scaleType="point" />
      </Chart>
    </Provider>
  );
}
```

The examples on this site follow the site's light and dark theme.

Spectrum color tokens, including the categorical colors in the default palette, have different values in light and dark. See [Color palettes](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/guides/color-palettes#categorical) for both sets of values.

### backgroundColor

`backgroundColor` fills the chart. It takes a Spectrum color token, like `gray-25`, or any CSS color, and defaults to `transparent`.

Some marks draw in the background color, like the outlines between donut segments and the fill behind a hovered line point. With a transparent background they use `gray-25` (white in light, `#111111` in dark). If the chart sits on a different color, set `backgroundColor` to that color so these details blend in.

## Palettes

`colors` sets the palette that a mark's `color` field draws from. Each series gets the next color in the order it first appears in `data`, and colors repeat when there are more series than colors. The default is `s2Categorical20`.

`colors` takes a named palette:

-   **Categorical** palettes, like `s2Categorical20`, are for unordered series.
-   **Sequential** palettes, like `sequentialViridis9`, are for ordered values, like low to high.
-   **Diverging** palettes, like `divergentRedBlue9`, are for values above and below a midpoint.

See [Color palettes](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/guides/color-palettes) for every palette and its colors.

### Custom colors

Pass a list instead of a name to choose the colors yourself. Each entry is a Spectrum color token or a CSS color:

```tsx
<Chart data={data} colors={['blue-900', 'magenta-900', '#0fb5ae', 'rgb(246, 133, 17)']}>
```

Spectrum color tokens switch to their dark value when `colorScheme` is `dark`; CSS colors stay the same. The tokens you can use are `gray-25` to `gray-1000`, `categorical-100` to `categorical-2000`, and `100` to `1600` of `silver`, `cinnamon`, `red`, `orange`, `yellow`, `brown`, `chartreuse`, `celery`, `green`, `seafoam`, `turquoise`, `cyan`, `blue`, `indigo`, `purple`, `fuchsia`, `pink`, and `magenta`. For sequential and diverging colors, use the named palettes.

### Color groups

`colors` also takes a list of lists: one group of colors per series. Marks that encode color with two fields use the first field to pick the group and the second to pick a color within it. On a `Bar`, for example, `color={['device', 'visitor']}` dodges by device and stacks by visitor, and each device keeps its own hue:

```tsx
<Chart
  data={barChannelVisitorData}
  colors={[
    ['blue-900', 'blue-500'],
    ['fuchsia-900', 'fuchsia-500'],
  ]}
>
  <Bar dimension="channel" metric="visits" color={['device', 'visitor']} type="dodged" />
  <Legend />
</Chart>
```

A group can be a named palette too, like `colors={['sequentialViridis5', 'sequentialMagma5']}`. See [Dodged and stacked](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/bar#dodged-and-stacked) for the full example.

## Other style scales

Color isn't the only thing a field can set. These `Chart` props are palettes for the other encodings, and work the same way as `colors`:

| Chart prop | Values | Default | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lineTypes` | `solid`, `dashed`, `dotted`, `dotDash`, `shortDash`, `longDash`, `twoDash`, or a dash array | `['solid', 'dashed', 'dotted', 'dotDash', 'longDash', 'twoDash']` | `lineType` on `Line`, `Bar`, `Scatter`, and `Legend` |
| `lineWidths` | `XS` to `XL`, or pixels | `['M']` | `lineWidth` on `Scatter` and `Legend` |
| `opacities` | Numbers from 0 to 1 | `[1]` | `opacity` on `Line`, `Bar`, `Scatter`, and `Legend` |
| `symbolShapes` | `rounded-square`, Vega symbol shapes like `circle`, or SVG paths | `['rounded-square']` | `symbolShape` on `Legend` |
| `symbolSizes` | A `[min, max]` pair of `XS` to `XL` or pixels | `['XS', 'XL']` | `size` on `Scatter`, which scales between the two |

`lineTypes` and `opacities` also take a list of lists for two-field encodings, like `colors`. See [Other scales](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#other-scales) for an example.

## Static and data-driven values

Encoding props like `color`, `lineType`, and `opacity` take either a field name or a fixed value:

-   A string is a field name. Each value in that field gets the next entry from the chart's palette, and an entry in the `Legend`.
-   `{ value: ... }` is a fixed value for every data point, like `{ value: 'gray-700' }` or `{ value: 0.5 }`. It doesn't use the palette.

```tsx
// One color per device, from the chart's colors
<Line dimension="month" metric="visits" color="device" scaleType="point" />

// Every line is dashed gray-700
<Line
  dimension="month"
  metric="visits"
  color={{ value: 'gray-700' }}
  lineType={{ value: 'dashed' }}
  scaleType="point"
/>
```

A fixed color can be a Spectrum color token or a CSS color, and tokens follow `colorScheme` the same way they do in `colors`.

## Beyond props

For styles the props don't cover, `config` merges into the chart's Vega config. See [config](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/chart#config).

---

# Color palettes

This page lists the palettes you can pass to `colors` on `Chart`. To set the palette, the color scheme, or your own colors, see [Colors and theming](/react-spectrum-charts/s2/docs/docs/guides/colors-and-theming).

## Categorical

Use categorical colors for series that have no order, like products or regions. Series get the colors in order, starting at A.

Each categorical color is a color from the [Spectrum 2 color palette](https://spectrum.adobe.com/page/color-palette/), like `indigo-1100`, and uses that color's light or dark value to match the chart's `colorScheme`.

| Category | Token | Spectrum color | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | `categorical-100` | `indigo-1100` | `#5424DB` | `#99A1FF` |
| B | `categorical-200` | `magenta-900` | `#D92361` | `#FF3377` |
| C | `categorical-300` | `orange-700` | `#E86A00` | `#B94900` |
| D | `categorical-400` | `blue-700` | `#5D89FF` | `#345BF8` |
| E | `categorical-500` | `purple-900` | `#9A47E2` | `#AD69E9` |
| F | `categorical-600` | `pink-700` | `#F24CB8` | `#C4278A` |
| G | `categorical-700` | `seafoam-700` | `#0BA286` | `#067A67` |
| H | `categorical-800` | `fuchsia-1000` | `#9C28AF` | `#E85BFD` |
| I | `categorical-900` | `green-1000` | `#036E45` | `#0EAF62` |
| J | `categorical-1000` | `celery-700` | `#52A119` | `#3C7A0F` |
| K | `categorical-1100` | `red-700` | `#FF513D` | `#CD2E1D` |
| L | `categorical-1200` | `cyan-1000` | `#046691` | `#269FF4` |
| M | `categorical-1300` | `silver-1200` | `#424242` | `#BEBEBE` |
| N | `categorical-1400` | `turquoise-1000` | `#056B74` | `#0DA8B6` |
| O | `categorical-1500` | `cinnamon-700` | `#C67E58` | `#A35834` |
| P | `categorical-1600` | `yellow-1000` | `#865500` | `#CB8D00` |
| Q | `categorical-1700` | `blue-1000` | `#274DEA` | `#6995FE` |
| R | `categorical-1800` | `seafoam-1000` | `#056C5C` | `#0CAD8E` |
| S | `categorical-1900` | `pink-500` | `#FF94DB` | `#8F1261` |
| T | `categorical-2000` | `red-1200` | `#811B0E` | `#FFA79D` |

There are four categorical palettes. Each one uses the first colors above, in order:

| Palette | Colors |
| --- | --- |
| `s2Categorical6` | A to F |
| `s2Categorical12` | A to L |
| `s2Categorical16` | A to P |
| `s2Categorical20` (default) | A to T |

Pick the smallest palette that covers your series. Colors repeat when there are more series than colors. To use one color on its own, pass its token: A is `categorical-100`, B is `categorical-200`, and so on, so `colors={['categorical-400']}` uses D.

## Sequential

> **Warning:**
> 
> Sequential and diverging palettes use the same colors in light and dark. Their colors in each theme are under review and expected to change.

Use sequential palettes for ordered values, like low to high. Each palette runs from light to dark, and the number at the end of the name is how many steps it has.

| Palette | Colors, in order |
| --- | --- |
| `sequentialViridis5` | rgb(253, 231, 37), rgb(122, 209, 81), rgb(31, 152, 139), rgb(57, 86, 140), rgb(68, 1, 84) |

| `sequentialMagma5` | rgb(254, 159, 109), rgb(252, 253, 191), rgb(196, 60, 117), rgb(87, 21, 126), rgb(0, 0, 4) |
| `sequentialMagma9` | rgb(252, 253, 191), rgb(253, 222, 160), rgb(254, 159, 109), rgb(241, 96, 93), rgb(196, 60, 117), rgb(140, 41, 129), rgb(87, 21, 126), rgb(32, 17, 75), rgb(0, 0, 4) |
| `sequentialMagma16` | rgb(252, 253, 191), rgb(253, 222, 160), rgb(254, 191, 132), rgb(254, 159, 109), rgb(250, 127, 94), rgb(241, 96, 93), rgb(222, 73, 104), rgb(196, 60, 117), rgb(168, 50, 125), rgb(140, 41, 129), rgb(114, 31, 129), rgb(87, 21, 126), rgb(59, 15, 112), rgb(32, 17, 75), rgb(11, 9, 36), rgb(0, 0, 4) |
